description: Official team representing SMKN 1 Jakarta (Boedoet) for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We specialize in software engineering, modern UI/UX design, and Earth data analytics using NASA open data. Our roster is currently reserved for internal Boedoet members.
summary:
HOLMES is an Earth-system detective. It turns a question about any city into a reproducible NASA data investigation and shows the answer on a globe.

The board maps 7,349 populated places in 228 countries to 6,561 MERRA-2 cells. Cached cells are colored by a NASA POWER trend,every other city is
 fetched and tested the first time someone inspects it. Pick a variable, a time window, and a season, and Holmes runs the full investigation: 45 years of monthly reanalysis data, Seasonal Sen slopes, Hamed-Rao Mann-Kendall, OLS with HAC errors, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control.

The city file is the evidence: a time-series chart with trend and 95% confidence interval, sparklines for every variable, p- and q-values, provenance, and plain-language caveats. NASA GIBS Then & Now shows the same city in 2001 and 2025. A NASA FIRMS 7-day snapshot adds active-fire detections, clearly labeled as detections, not confirmed wildfires.

Holmes is designed to be honest. 'Not significant', 'mixed signal', and 'insufficient data' are first-class results. A marker is a MERRA-2 cell, not a city boundary. Board q-values apply only to cached cells. Every number comes from the deterministic stats engine.
details:
HOLMES is a climate trend investigation tool built for NASA Space Apps 2026. It turns NASA climate data into a city-level evidence file that a non-specialist can read and a specialist can audit.

What exactly does it do?

HOLMES answers a simple question: what changed, where, by how much, and how strong is the evidence?

A user can:

1. Choose a climate variable, such as temperature, rainfall, soil wetness, humidity, wind, solar radiation, or aerosol optical depth.

2. Choose a place from 121 cities in 62 countries, with a strong focus on Indonesia.

3. Choose a time window: the full 1981 to 2025 record, or the last 35, 25, or 15 years.

4. Choose a season: all year, DJF, MAM, JJA, or SON.

5. Read the result through four map lenses:

• Effect: trend size.

• Evidence: statistical confidence after FDR correction.

• Agreement: whether selected variables move together.

• Coverage: how much of the expected record is present.

The globe is for discovery. Clicking a city opens its evidence file, which contains:

• A plain-language verdict, such as warming, cooling, wetter, drying, or cleaner air.

• Sen slope per decade.

• A 95% confidence interval.

• p-values and FDR-adjusted q-values.

• Number of years and months used.

• A method-dependence warning when statistical tests disagree.

• An evidence stack with sparklines for key variables.

• An interactive time-series chart with raw, deseasonalized, and annual views.

• Provenance, citation, license, and caveats.

The site also includes:

• Then and Now satellite comparisons for Jakarta and Wisconsin.

• Fire Watch with NASA FIRMS hot-pixel clusters.

• Six starter cases.

• A feature tour.

• Shareable deep links that preserve the current view.

How does it work?

HOLMES has four layers.

1. Data acquisition

scripts/fetch_power.py calls the NASA POWER monthly point API for 121 city coordinates. It requests 10 parameters from 1981 to 2025 and caches each raw response as JSON.

The parameters cover:

• Air temperature, minimum temperature, and maximum temperature.

• Corrected precipitation.

• Root-zone and surface soil wetness.

• Relative humidity.

• Wind speed.

• All-sky shortwave radiation.

• Aerosol optical depth at 550 nm.

2. Precomputation

scripts/prewarm.py builds the monthly series and runs every city, variable, time window, and season combination through the statistics engine.

The outputs are:

• series.json: monthly values for charting.

• city-trends.json: precomputed trend statistics for every city, variable, window, and season.

• The UI reads these precomputed results, so city files and map colors load instantly.

3. Statistics engine

The FastAPI service in apps/stats-engine computes:

• Seasonal Sen slope, reported per decade.

• Hamed-Rao Mann-Kendall trend test after removing the seasonal cycle.

• Theil-Sen confidence intervals.

• OLS with HAC standard errors as an independent cross-check.

• Minimum-year and completeness checks.

• Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.

• Evidence levels: strong, moderate, weak, or insufficient.

• Standardized slopes for multi-variable composites.

A result is marked method-dependent when the Mann-Kendall and OLS-HAC tests disagree.

4. Web application

The web app is a React and TypeScript single-page application. MapLibre GL renders the globe, country boundaries, city footprints, fire detections, city labels, and the day-night terminator. uPlot renders the time-series chart.

The app can read bundled static JSON or query an optional Convex backend. The static path makes the demo reliable without network dependencies.

What benefits does it have?

For users:

• Fast local answers: open a city and get a verdict without building a data pipeline.

• Understandable evidence: a plain-language verdict, a chart, and an evidence stack sit next to the statistics.

• Visible uncertainty: confidence intervals, p-values, q-values, coverage, and caveats are shown, not hidden.

• Fair comparison: the same method is applied consistently across cities, variables, windows, and seasons.

• Multi-variable thinking: users can combine variables to see whether heat, water, and air signals agree.

• Shareable findings: a URL preserves the exact city, variable, window, season, lens, and layers.

For public communication:

• It separates association from causation.

• It separates a grid-cell trend from a weather-station measurement.

• It distinguishes a fire detection from a confirmed wildfire.

• It makes the method and its limits part of the product.

For engineering:

• Precomputed data keeps the demo fast and deterministic.

• The statistics service is stateless and independently testable.

• The web client can fall back to static data if Convex is unavailable.

• The method version is explicit, so results can be reproduced.

• The repository includes unit tests, contract tests, and a Playwright smoke-test script.

What do you hope to achieve?

The immediate goal is to help a user move from a global question to a local, defensible answer in under a minute.

The broader goals are:

• Improve climate literacy by showing how trends are measured and questioned.

• Reduce overclaiming by making uncertainty and caveats visible.

• Give students, educators, journalists, and local analysts a practical evidence tool.

• Prove a transparent pipeline that can scale to more cities, variables, and NASA datasets.

• Add live data refresh, more satellite Then and Now comparisons, report export, localization, and stronger mobile support in future versions.

HOLMES is not a forecast and does not claim causation. It is an evidence workspace.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

Languages:

• TypeScript • HTML • JSON

• Python • CSS • Bash

Frontend:

• React 19 • uPlot • Framer Motion

• Vite 7 • MapLibre GL JS 5 • Lucide React

• Tailwind CSS 4 • driver.js

Backend and data:

• Convex for optional hosted queries, schema, and seeding

• FastAPI and Uvicorn for the statistics service

• Pydantic for request and response models

• NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, and pymannkendall for the statistics

• Docker and Fly.io configuration for deploying the stats engine

Development and testing:

• pnpm 10 • pytest • Playwright smoke-test script

• Nx 21 • uv

• Vitest • Github

Hardware

No custom hardware is required. The app runs in a modern browser with WebGL2 for the globe. The statistics engine runs in a standard cloud container. Development and demonstration work on an ordinary laptop.

Why Holmes Is the Shape of Our Creative

• Evidence files, not just maps: Clicking any of the 121 cities opens full stats, caveats, and time-series charts.

• Two audiences, one UI: Progressive disclosure pairs plain verdicts (WARMING) with deep scientific metrics.

• Honest uncertainty: Explicit evidence tiers (STRONG to INSUFFICIENT) and METHOD-DEPENDENT flags prevent false certainty.

• Four lenses & multi-variable: View Effect, Evidence, Agreement, and Coverage across single or combined climate signals.

• Three NASA datasets: Integrates POWER/MERRA-2 (climate), FIRMS (fire), and GIBS (satellite imagery) in one view.

• Reproducible & transparent: Versioned methods, strict no-forecast boundaries, and state-preserving share links.

• Earth System Detective UX: Fast, precomputed HUD interface with guided tours and starter cases.

Factors Considered in Holmes

• Scientific rigor: Deseasonalized Hamed-Rao Mann-Kendall tests, OLS-HAC cross-checks, and FDR corrections.

• Ethical & data limits: Clear caveats on grid resolution (~55×69 km), missing data, and trend vs. forecast boundaries.

• Broad accessibility: Plain-language labels, keyboard shortcuts, and mobile-friendly layouts for both citizens and analysts.

• Instant performance: Precomputed trends, static JSON fallbacks, MapLibre, and uPlot eliminate server wait times.

• Modular & focused: Decoupled FastAPI backend for easy scaling while keeping the core investigation path streamlined.

What it does not do

• It does not forecast future climate.

• It does not claim that a trend proves causation.
